passage:
"Pallavi, you're my best friend. So you can't play with the new girl."

Pallavi looked at the new girl, standing alone by the sandpit. "But she's got a bucket."

"Best friends only play with each other," Yamini insisted, grabbing Pallavi's arm.

Their teacher crouched beside them. "Yamini, you and Pallavi are very close. That's lovely. Can best friends play with someone else too?"

Yamini frowned. "Then Pallavi won't like me as much."

"Does your Amma love you less when she talks to your Nani?"

"...No."

"Shall we ask the new girl to build a castle with you both?"

Yamini sighed. "Okay. But I'm doing the tower."

qa.q: Where was the new girl standing?
qa.a: Alone by the sandpit.

qa.q: Why did Yamini want Pallavi to play only with her?
qa.a: She was most likely worried that sharing Pallavi would mean being liked less; she said so herself. Grabbing Pallavi's arm shows how strongly she wanted to hold on to her friend.

qa.q: How did the teacher help Yamini see that closeness can include others?
qa.a: The teacher praised their friendship, then used an everyday example about Amma and Nani, and suggested building a castle together.

qa.q: How might the new girl feel while Yamini keeps Pallavi to herself?
qa.a: She is probably lonely and left out, standing alone with her bucket, hoping someone will let her join.

grounding: It shows a young child calling someone her best friend and excluding another child, and an adult teaching that closeness can include others.

subtype: Saying I love you and drawing [Expressing]
passage:
In the kitchen in Seville, Hana handed Pablo a crumpled drawing: a tall stick man with a huge red heart for a body.

"That's you, Abuelo. I love you forever and ever, a hundred million."

Pablo pinned it to the fridge with the lemon magnet. "And I love you."

An hour later, when he said it was bath time, Hana stamped her foot. "I don't love you anymore!"

Pablo just ran the water.

Wrapped in a towel afterwards, she climbed onto his lap. "I love you again. And I love the ice-cream man too."

Pablo laughed. "Of course you do."

qa.q: What did Pablo use to pin the drawing to the fridge?
qa.a: The lemon magnet.

qa.q: What was Hana feeling when she said, "I don't love you anymore!"?
qa.a: She was most likely annoyed and frustrated about bath time, and her words showed that feeling in the moment, not a real change in love. Climbing onto his lap later shows she still felt close to him.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Pablo didn't take the angry words to heart and just ran the bath, because he understood they were a flash of feeling, not a promise.

qa.q: How does Pablo see Hana's "I love you forever" and "I don't love you anymore"?
qa.a: He sees both as big feelings of the moment, so he enjoys the love and laughs off the anger.

grounding: It shows a preschooler saying "I love you" and drawing a picture for her grandfather, with words that carry strong feelings in the moment rather than fixed promises.

passage:
At the art table in the preschool, Shalini watched Chandrika paint a rainbow with a smiling sun. "Wow! You draw so good!" she said, and started painting a rainbow and sun of her own, exactly the same.

After snack time, Chandrika sat with two other children at a new table and they laughed together.

Shalini looked over, then back at her own painting. When Chandrika came to fetch her brush, Shalini said, "Your rainbow's ugly. Mine's better."

Chandrika's face fell. The teacher came and knelt between them. "Shalini, earlier you loved Chandrika's rainbow. Are you feeling left out?"

Shalini nodded, eyes down.

qa.q: What did Chandrika paint?
qa.a: A rainbow with a smiling sun.

qa.q: Why did Shalini say Chandrika's rainbow was ugly?
qa.a: She was most likely feeling left out and a bit jealous when Chandrika sat with other children, so her admiration flipped to rivalry. Her nod with eyes down suggests she felt ashamed too.

qa.q: How did the teacher help?
qa.a: The teacher reminded Shalini of her earlier praise and gently named the likely feeling, left out, instead of just scolding the unkind words.

qa.q: What is it like for Chandrika to hear her rainbow called ugly?
qa.a: It hurts and confuses her, since the same friend praised it earlier; her face falls.

grounding: It shows a preschooler praising and copying a friend's painting, then flipping to rivalry when she feels left out.

passage:
"Mama, look at my tower!"

Reena didn't look up from her phone. "Good job."

Tushar's smile faded. "You didn't even look."

"I did, beta..."

"You didn't. Your face didn't move."

Reena put the phone down and came over. She crouched and really looked. "Oh, I see. You put the big blocks at the bottom so it doesn't wobble. And you made a flag from paper on the top."

Tushar's smile came back. "The flag was the hardest part!"

"I can tell. You tried three times, didn't you?"

"Four!"

qa.q: What did Tushar make from paper for the top of the tower?
qa.a: A flag.

qa.q: How did Tushar feel when Reena said "Good job" without looking?
qa.a: He felt disappointed and hurt, because he read her flat face and voice as not really caring. His smile faded before he said so.

qa.q: Why did Reena's second praise land better?
qa.a: It was specific about what he had done, big blocks at the bottom and the paper flag, and she was really looking, so it felt real and noticed his effort.

qa.q: How does Reena see the moment when Tushar says "Your face didn't move"?
qa.a: She is probably a bit caught out and sorry, which is why she puts the phone down and gives him her full attention.

grounding: It shows a young child reading flat praise as empty from tone and face, and specific words about what he did landing better.

subtype: Accepting comfort from a trusted adult [Regulating]
passage:
The storm knocked out the power just as the thunder cracked right overhead. Bhavna screamed and ran to Damini Masi, sobbing.

Their neighbour, sheltering in the doorway, said, "Arre, stop crying, it's only noise."

Damini Masi pulled her niece onto her lap in the dark and held her close. "That was so loud. You were scared. Of course you were." She rocked slowly. "I'm here. We're safe inside."

Bhavna's sobs slowed to hiccups. "It went BOOM," she whispered.

"It did. A big boom. You were scared, and now you're a bit less scared."

Bhavna nodded against her shoulder.

qa.q: Who said "stop crying, it's only noise"?
qa.a: Their neighbour, sheltering in the doorway.

qa.q: What was Bhavna feeling when she ran to Damini Masi sobbing?
qa.a: She was frightened by the sudden crack of thunder in the dark. As she was held and her fear was named, she became calmer, slowing to hiccups.

qa.q: Why did Damini Masi's response help more than the neighbour's?
qa.a: Holding Bhavna and naming the feeling, "You were scared," helped her settle and learn a word for it, whereas "stop crying" would teach her to hide it.

qa.q: What would change if Damini Masi had agreed with the neighbour?
qa.a: Bhavna might have tried to hide her fear, stayed frightened, and learnt that her feelings are not welcome.

grounding: It shows a young child settling in a trusted adult's lap after a fright, with the adult naming the fear instead of telling her to stop crying.

passage:
Lalit sat on the step, crying. His ice cream lay melting on the ground.

Shreya ran over and patted his back hard. "Don't cry, I'm here! You can have my car. Look, it's red!"

"Go away," Lalit sobbed, turning his shoulder.

Shreya looked hurt. "But I'm helping!"

Her mother, sitting nearby, called softly, "Shreya, come here a sec." She whispered, "You were so kind. Sometimes people want a little space first. Shall we wait here, and you can offer the car later?"

Shreya sat with her mother, watching Lalit. After a while, he looked over. "Can I see the car?"

qa.q: What lay melting on the ground?
qa.a: His ice cream.

qa.q: What was Shreya feeling when Lalit said "Go away"?
qa.a: She felt hurt and confused, because she was sincerely trying to help and he pushed her away. Her "But I'm helping!" shows she didn't yet understand he wanted space.

qa.q: How did Shreya's mother help her?
qa.a: She praised Shreya's kindness and explained that people sometimes want space first, suggesting she wait and offer the car later.

qa.q: If you were Lalit, what might you want right after dropping the ice cream?
qa.a: A little time to be sad without someone patting you, and then maybe some company, as Lalit shows when he asks to see the car.

grounding: It shows a preschooler offering sincere, concrete comfort to a sad friend without yet knowing when someone wants space instead.

subtype: Reading whether an apology is meant [Interpreting]
passage:
Under the big tree in the hill village, the children were queueing for the rope swing. Lalremsiami pushed in front of Bidisha, knocking her sideways.

"Say sorry," someone called.

"Sorry," Lalremsiami muttered, grinning at her friends, and didn't move.

"Okay," said Bidisha, and stood behind her.

Bidisha's Nani, sorting beans on her porch, called her over. "Did she mean that sorry?"

Bidisha shrugged. "She said it."

"Look. Is she giving your turn back?"

Bidisha looked. Lalremsiami was already swinging. "No."

"Then it isn't fixed yet. Let's go and talk to them together."

qa.q: What was Bidisha's Nani sorting on her porch?
qa.a: Beans.

qa.q: What was Bidisha feeling when she said "Okay" and stood behind?
qa.a: She probably felt a bit hurt at being pushed, but accepted the "sorry" at face value, trusting that the word fixed things. Her shrug suggests she was unsure what else to expect.

qa.q: How did Nani help Bidisha check whether repair had happened?
qa.a: She asked Bidisha to look at whether Lalremsiami gave the turn back, so Bidisha could see the behaviour hadn't changed, and then offered to talk to them together.

qa.q: How does Lalremsiami treat the apology?
qa.a: She treats it as a word to get out of trouble: she mutters it while grinning at her friends and keeps the turn.

grounding: It shows a young child accepting a "sorry" at face value and an adult helping her check tone and whether the behaviour stopped.

passage:
Crash! Bablu's block tower fell across the floor. Mahima stood over it, holding the block she had grabbed.

"Sorry!" she said fast, and turned to run off.

"Wait a moment, Mahima," said Ankita Mausi. "Come and sit with me."

Mahima sat, looking at her knees.

"What happened to Bablu's tower?"

"It fell. I took the red block."

"How do you think he feels?"

Mahima looked at her cousin. He was crying quietly. "Sad."

"What could help fix it?"

Mahima thought. Then she went over, held out the red block and said, "I'll help you build it again."

qa.q: Which block did Mahima take?
qa.a: The red block.

qa.q: What was Mahima feeling when she said "Sorry!" fast and turned to run?
qa.a: She was most likely nervous about being in trouble and wanted the conflict to end quickly. Looking at her knees suggests she also felt a little ashamed.

qa.q: What did Ankita Mausi do instead of forcing a quick apology?
qa.a: She helped Mahima notice what happened, who was hurt and how Bablu felt, and then asked what could fix it, so Mahima chose a real repair.

qa.q: How is Bablu affected by the first quick "Sorry"?
qa.a: It doesn't help him; he is still crying over his fallen tower until Mahima offers to rebuild it with him.

grounding: It shows a preschooler saying a quick sorry to end a conflict, and an adult helping her understand who was hurt and how to fix it.

passage:
"Mumma, my tummy hurts. And I'm cross."

Anjali knelt beside Sumit. "Show me where it hurts."

He waved a hand all over his middle. "Everywhere."

"Is it a hungry hurt or an ouchy hurt?"

Sumit thought, rubbing his eyes. "Hungry... and sleepy."

"You didn't eat much lunch. Let's have some rice first."

He ate half a bowl, yawned hugely and curled up on the sofa. Five minutes later he was asleep.

Anjali pulled a sheet over him. When he woke she would ask again, and if his tummy still hurt or anything worried her, she would call the doctor.

qa.q: What did Anjali give Sumit to eat?
qa.a: Some rice.

qa.q: What was Sumit most likely feeling when he said his tummy hurt and he was cross?
qa.a: He was most likely hungry and very tired, which came out as crankiness and a vague tummy ache; rubbing his eyes and falling asleep fast support this. A real pain was also possible, so it needed checking.

qa.q: How did Anjali take the tummy report seriously?
qa.a: She asked where it hurt, offered simple choices to describe it, and planned to ask again after his sleep and call the doctor if it still hurt or worried her.

qa.q: What would change if Anjali had said, "Stop being cross"?
qa.a: Sumit might not have been fed or rested, and she could have missed whether his tummy was really hurting.

grounding: It shows a preschooler mixing hunger, tiredness and a tummy ache in his words, and an adult asking where it hurts and noticing the tiredness.

subtype: Reading a child's unmet need behind behaviour [Interpreting]
passage:
The birthday party in the colony hall was loud: music, balloons popping, twenty children running. Omkar clung to Lalremsiami Aunty's leg and whined at everything.

She ran through the possibilities in her head. Hungry? He'd had pakoras. Tired? Maybe. Too much noise? His hands kept going to his ears.

She crouched. "Omkar, do you want a snack, or a quiet corner?"

He pointed at the door. "Quiet."

They sat on the steps outside. After a few minutes he let go of her leg and started counting the pigeons.

"Better?" He nodded. "Want to go back in?" "In a bit."

qa.q: What did Omkar start counting on the steps?
qa.a: The pigeons.

qa.q: What was Omkar probably feeling when he clung and whined at the party?
qa.a: He was most likely overwhelmed by the noise, since his hands kept going to his ears and he chose the quiet steps. Tiredness might also have been part of it.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Lalremsiami Aunty treated her guesses as guesses and offered a simple choice, snack or quiet corner, which let Omkar show what he needed.

qa.q: How might the loud party look different to the other children?
qa.a: For many of them the noise and balloons are fun and exciting, while for Omkar the same party feels like too much.

grounding: It shows an adult reading a clingy child's crankiness by weighing hunger, tiredness and overstimulation, then confirming with a simple choice.
